openings.text: Ada hurried into the roof garden with three invitations tucked under her arm. The moonmelon party needed guests, and Ada wanted every card to arrive neat as a button.
Ada looked up and found the invitations pinned high on the roof post. “Oh dear,” she said. “The wind has made a bulletin board!”
Ada peeked into the wicker basket and discovered a paper lantern nestled beside the invitations. Its moon-shaped handle tickled her nose.
Pip stretched his wings toward the roof tiles. Ada noticed that he was imagining a grand flying delivery, although she had imagined something much neater.
The invitations waited on the little party table, the basket was plain, and Pip had his quietest toes ready. Ada smiled. This might be a wonderfully ordinary delivery.

variants.text: Ada shaded her eyes and inspected the tall post. She discovered that the wind had pinned the three invitations there, fluttering like tiny white flags.
Ada inspected the tall post. No invitations were pinned there; they were still waiting safely on the party table.
Ada opened the basket and discovered a paper lantern tucked among the invitations. “A glow-up for our party!” she whispered.
Ada opened the basket and discovered only the invitations inside. “Plain and ready,” she said, giving the basket a pleased little tap.
Ada watched Pip’s wings wobble with excitement and discovered that he was expecting a grand flying delivery. His tail drew imaginary loops in the air.
Ada watched Pip fold his wings carefully and discovered that he was not expecting a flying delivery. His toes stood ready for a quiet job.
Ada faced Pip. “I want the invitations delivered neatly,” she said. “No card upside down, no guest chased by a dragon, and only a teeny-tiny flourish.” Pip listened closely.
Ada handed Pip the blue ribbon. Pip held it between two careful claws. “A ribbon for a ribbon-worthy mission!” he declared.
Pip tied the blue ribbon around the wind-pinned invitations. The roof post suddenly looked dressed for dancing, and the cards stopped flapping like startled minnows.
Ada pressed the invitations neatly against the ribboned roof post. “There,” she said. “A delivery with its shoes polished.”
Pip lifted the plain basket with extremely serious dragon toes. “I can carry a basket without tickling it!” he announced, while Ada tried not to laugh at his solemn face.
At the moonmelon trellis, Pip set the basket down and smoothed one bent-looking—though perfectly sound—handle. Ada gathered the invitations for the next step.
Ada carried the plain invitations along the quiet roof-garden path. Pip marched beside her, whispering, “Left foot, right foot, absolutely no dramatic swooping.”
Ada carried the basket beneath the moonmelon trellis. The paper lantern stayed safe among the invitations, waiting like a sleepy moon for its evening glow.
Ada lit the paper lantern beside the delivered invitations. Warm gold spilled over the trellis, and every moonmelon seemed to grow a little smile.
Ada told Pip, “I know you hoped for a grand flight. My neat plan can have one small flourish.” Pip’s eyes grew round. “A tidy swoop?” he asked.
Pip understood at last. “Neat first, spectacular second?” he asked. Ada nodded. “A tiny air-mail show.” Pip tucked the ribbon close and grinned with all his little dragon teeth.
Pip swept upward in one careful flap. The three invitations floated down on the blue ribbon, looping once around the trellis before landing exactly where Jun could catch them.
Pip returned the blue ribbon to Ada with a bow so deep that his nose brushed the roof tiles.
Jun climbed into the roof garden, holding an invitation high. “Splendid delivery!” Jun called, whether it had arrived by post, path, or dragon-powered air.
Jun looked from the invitation to Ada and Pip. The card had truly arrived, and Jun’s smile became as wide as a moonmelon slice.
Ada rang the tiny brass bell. Ting! The moonmelon party began, bright and bouncy beneath the open sky.

endings.text: The ribboned invitations fluttered on the roof post while Jun climbed up laughing, one hand raised to catch the next little shiver of paper.
The roof post wore its blue ribbon proudly. Jun arrived laughing beneath it, and the invitations bobbed overhead like three tiny flags.
The lit lantern glowed under the trellis, and the invitations rested safely beside its moon-shaped handle. Gold light trembled on Jun’s delighted cheeks.
Under the glowing trellis lantern, Jun found the invitations beside the moon-shaped handle and reached for one as the light hummed softly.
The blue ribbon looped through the air as Pip landed beside Jun, who held the invitation like a tiny flag. Pip’s wings folded into a proud, tidy zigzag.
Pip settled beside Jun, and the blue-ribbon air-mail curled between them. Jun waved the invitation overhead while Pip’s little wings gave one last happy flap.
